analysis.one_liner: Forces drug companies to make the same data and patent disclosures to the patent office that they make to the FDA.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee: referred on September 13, 2023, it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies seeking or holding FDA approval for a drug or biologic to tell the patent office everything they tell the FDA — and vice versa — about data and patents, and to certify that the two records match. If a company carelessly or deliberately leaves something out, competitors could use that as a defense if the company sues them for patent infringement. The goal is to stop drugmakers from winning longer or broader patents by telling the patent office one story and the FDA another.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay brand-name drug prices would gain, because the bill makes it harder for drugmakers to win or defend patents using claims inconsistent with the data they gave the FDA — the kind of inconsistencies that keep cheaper generic and biosimilar competitors off the market. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers would also gain, getting a legal defense against patents their rivals obtained without full disclosure.

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug sponsors and license holders to submit to the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office any information material to patentability that they give the FDA, and to certify to each agency that the information they provided the other is complete and consistent.

Creates a legal defense for anyone accused of infringing a drug patent if the patent owner negligently or intentionally failed to make the required disclosures, weakening patents won through inconsistent statements.
Lets the FDA refuse to approve a drug application whose sponsor is out of compliance with the new disclosure requirements, and makes noncompliance a prohibited act the FDA can enforce.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies would bear the cost: they would have to certify, on pain of having applications denied, that what they tell the patent office matches what they tell the FDA, and any patent obtained or defended after a careless or intentional failure to disclose could become unenforceable against competitors.

drawbacks.text: The penalty for noncompliance is severe and partly automatic: a sponsor who negligently fails a disclosure requirement can face denial of its drug application, and a patent holder's mere negligent omission can render a valid patent unenforceable, raising the risk that good-faith paperwork errors kill useful medicines' exclusivity.

The bill adds a new dual-reporting and certification burden on every new drug application and every applicable patent, which could slow filings and add compliance costs, some of which drugmakers may pass along.
The disclosure duty covers only patents tied to a given FDA application, so the broader problem of patent thickets and evergreening through separate filings would remain largely unaddressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: more consistent disclosures should make some improperly obtained patents easier to challenge, speeding generic and biosimilar competition and lowering drug prices. The cost is a heavier compliance burden on drug sponsors and harsh, partly automatic penalties — application denial for certification failures and unenforceable patents for negligent omissions — that could deter legitimate filings. The bill is a narrow tool for a large problem: it would not touch most patent-thicket strategies, and its fate suggests even this modest step faced resistance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in House committees for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in September 2023 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, with its health provisions sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, in either the House or the Senate.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, leaving drugmakers' FDA and patent-office disclosures unlinked as before.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the existing ability to make different, potentially inconsistent claims about data and patents to the FDA and the patent office was left untouched, and no new disclosure duties or patent-enforcement penalties were created. Patients waiting for cheaper generics and biosimilars gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Ann Kuster (D-NH)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring drugmakers to make consistent disclosures to the FDA and the patent office.

for.name: Rep. Diana Harshbarger (R-TN)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a Republican co-sponsor.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: After the bill was referred to the committee on September 13, 2023, no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill's shared referral in the patent jurisdiction without any markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with one Republican cosponsor, but no vote was ever taken, so the parties' actual split is unknown.

industries.note: The bill targets the practice of describing the same drug data differently to the patent office than to the FDA in order to obtain or defend patents that block generic competition. Its certification duty, application-denial penalty, and new infringement defense all cut into that practice, and the industry's interest in the bill ran against patients paying brand prices.

A new statutory defense would let generic and biosimilar makers escape infringement liability on patents whose owners failed to make required disclosures, making it easier to launch lower-priced copies.
